coverage.notes: Lab memos and computer-problem reports are covered by a written instructor memo spec, two readable lab prompts, both computer-problem prompts, and completed examples. The first computer-problem prompt is an image-only scan with no text layer; it was read as an image, so its tool rules are now confirmed rather than inferred from the second. Homework survives only as prompts with bare answers in the location searched. Exams and equation sheets are image-only scans and are out of scope.

course_policy.summary: This course has had a stated generative-AI policy. Its current terms are unknown.
course_policy.notes: Course-wide policy is unknown and stays that way. One assignment family is not unknown: see assignment_families, computer-problem, ai_use, where the prompt itself prohibits AI assistance and the pack requires a hard stop. That is assignment-specific evidence and is not read across to labs or homework. A host reading this block must check that family before helping with a computer problem.

precedence: the instructor's written technical-memo format spec

typography.line_spacing_note: 1.5 is the stated preference for lab reports; the general memo spec accepts single spacing.

abstract.content: objective, method in a phrase, and the key numerical results with units

page_numbering.first_numbered_page: first page of the body (title page is unnumbered and does not count)

body.length_note: Lab memos: the body is exactly two full pages, and figures inside it count. The general memo spec allows 1-2 pages; use the assignment prompt's number when it gives one.
sections_observed: Introduction and Methods (or separate Objectives and Methods)
sections_required_by_spec: indication of methods (not a full description)
description of results shown in the figures
body.no_trailing_whitespace: No body page should end with a large empty block, and no graph should take a full page when the body is limited to two pages.

equations.numbering: sequential, numbered at the right margin
equations.label_style_note: The spec requires right-margin numbering but not a particular label form. The instructor's own handouts use (N), and one completed memo uses [Equation N]. Either form satisfies the spec; use one form consistently.
equations.placement: Inline at the point of first use and explained in context, like a textbook. Never collected into an appendix list.
forbidden: code-style notation such as ^ or * in displayed math

figures.numbering: in order of first reference in the text, placed where first referenced
plot_rules: no chart title inside the graph when the figure is captioned
axis labels with units, lettering readable when projected
one plotted line per graph when the prompt asks for a single best fit
caption describes the content, not the form 'Y vs X'
figures.schematic_rules: Drawn digitally (simple shapes are fine), every relevant component labeled, no hand drawing.
figures.source: memo spec + lab prompt + peer-review checklist

rules: sensible significant digits (2-3 for measured data)

appendices.labeling: lettered (Appendix A, B, ...), with a heading on each page
contents: more detailed method description if needed
rules: spreadsheet data only in digested, readable form, never a raw dump
no page that is only a list of equations
appendices.source: memo spec + lab prompt + computer-problem prompt

voice.person: third person; no I, we, you, 'the team', or 'the author' in lab reports
voice.tone: concise and non-narrative; no diary-style storytelling
voice.scope_note: The first-person ban is stated for lab reports. Completed group computer-problem reports used 'we'; whether that is acceptable there is unconfirmed.

units_and_numbers.unit_typesetting: superscripts and subscripts (m3 with a raised 3), never ^ notation
units_and_numbers.greek_letters: real Greek glyphs, not spelled-out names
units_and_numbers.significant_digits: reasonable for the measurement, typically 2-3 for experimental data, including appendices and graph labels

tooling.labs: Excel for all data reduction and calculation, Word (equation editor) for the memo. The prompt discourages hand calculation.
tooling.computer_problems: EES preferred. Use one property source throughout: either the tool's built-in property functions or the textbook tables, never both. Both prompts state the preference and the no-mixing rule in their own words, so both are confirmed rather than inferred.

computer_problems_accepted_tools.note: The two prompts give different accepted lists: only the second names MATLAB. This is a real divergence between assignments, not an error, so it is recorded per prompt rather than merged. Follow the list in the prompt for the assignment at hand, and where it is silent, prefer EES.
computer_problems_accepted_tools.hand_calculation: The first prompt allows hand calculation as a check but grades only work done in the chosen application.

tooling.computer_problems_confidence: both prompts read directly; the first is an image-only scan with no text layer and was read as an image
tooling.property_tables: Cengel textbook appendix tables (SI and English), cited as the source when used

submission.labs: draft for peer review, then final PDF upload; printed copy stapled
submission.computer_problems: electronic copy plus a paper printout of the electronic work

methods.title: State-point analysis with property tables
methods.when: Any cycle or device analysis (compressors, turbines, valves, heat exchangers, refrigeration and power cycles).
steps: Draw the system and number every state point; mark which states share a pressure and which process connects each pair (isentropic, isenthalpic throttle, constant pressure).
Tabulate the known properties at each state and name the table each missing property will come from (saturated, superheated, compressed liquid).
Fix each state with two independent properties, then read or interpolate T, P, v, h, s, showing the interpolation.
For non-ideal devices, find the isentropic state first (the 2s state) and then apply the isentropic efficiency to get the actual state.
Apply mass and energy balances per device, carrying units through every line.
Report the cycle metrics (heat rates, work, COP or efficiency) with units, and show the states on a T-s or P-h diagram.
pitfalls: Mixing a software package's property functions with textbook table values in the same analysis.
Using the isentropic state as the actual state, or applying the efficiency in the wrong direction for a compressor versus a turbine.
Dropping units partway through; units are expected on every homework and test answer.
Interpolating across a phase boundary instead of switching tables.

methods.title: Lab data reduction in Excel
methods.when: Every lab. The prompt expects all supporting math in a spreadsheet, not by hand.
steps: Before the lab, list every equation and every variable it needs, and build the data sheet from that list.
Record the zero offsets of any gauge that should read zero before flow or heating starts, then subtract them in the analysis.
Convert every input to one consistent unit system in its own column, and convert temperatures to absolute before any radiation or ratio calculation.
Write each formula once and fill it across all runs or data points instead of repeating arithmetic.
Set display precision in the spreadsheet so results show sensible significant digits without losing the underlying precision.
pitfalls: An isolated unit-conversion slip in one input cell (a Fahrenheit-to-kelvin factor, for example) that propagates silently into every result; check every converted input against an independent conversion.
Pasting thousands of raw rows into the appendix instead of a digested table.

methods.title: Calibration constant as the slope of actual versus ideal
methods.when: A single correction or conversion factor relates two measured quantities (a discharge coefficient, or a sensor's volts-per-watt constant).
steps: Compute the ideal or reference quantity and the measured quantity at each operating point.
Plot measured (y) against ideal (x) with markers only.
Fit a line through the origin; the slope is the single calibration constant.
Report one constant with units, and note which points are least trustworthy (usually the lowest-signal ones).
pitfalls: Averaging point-by-point ratios instead of taking the slope when the prompt asks for a slope.
Using a published value in the analysis or on the graph when the prompt allows it only as a comparison in the text.

methods.title: Parameter sweep to minimize error or cost
methods.when: A model has one unknown parameter to fit to data (a cooling time constant, say), or a design has parameters to optimize (pressure, efficiency, surface choices) and no closed form is expected.
steps: Write the model or cost function with the free parameter(s) explicit.
Sweep the parameter over a sensible range in the spreadsheet or tool, computing the objective (sum of squared error against all data points, or total cost) at each value.
Refine the step size around the minimum.
Show the result with a graph that proves it: the objective against the parameter, or the best-fit model over the data.
State the chosen value and why, and check that it meets every stated constraint.
pitfalls: Fitting to a subset of the data instead of every point.
An error-versus-parameter plot whose axis runs negative; a sum of squares cannot be below zero, so that points to a plotting or formula error.
Several model lines on one graph when the prompt asks for only one.

methods.title: Radiation exchange with view factors
methods.when: Surface radiation problems: emissivity measurement, spacecraft or enclosure energy balances.
steps: Draw the geometry and identify every surface pair that exchanges radiation, with areas and distances.
Get each view factor from the appropriate relation or chart, applying reciprocity and summation checks.
Write the net exchange with absolute temperatures to the fourth power.
Close the steady-state energy balance on the body, including internal generation.
Compare measured or chosen emissivities against a cited handbook value or range from the course heat-transfer text.
pitfalls: Using Celsius or Fahrenheit inside a T^4 term.
Claiming agreement with an uncited or unspecified 'online value'. When the prompt requires a reference value on the graph, it must actually appear there, with its source.
Substituting a handbook value for a different surface finish without saying so; when the exact finish is not tabulated, report the bracketing range instead.

assignment_families.title: Laboratory technical memo
stages: pre-lab: list the governing equations and prepare a data sheet from them
lab session: collect data as a group
individual analysis in Excel (no sharing of processed data)
draft memo brought to class for peer review against a checklist
deliverables: lettered appendices with the scanned raw data sheet and detailed calculations
supporting Excel workbook (kept by the author, not submitted)
what_good_looks_like: The abstract states the objective and gives the key numerical results with units, so a reader could stop there.
The body fills exactly two pages, with every analysis item the prompt enumerates addressed there, and nothing cut to the appendix that the prompt requires in the body.
A clean digital apparatus schematic with every relevant component labeled.
Each key equation appears once, numbered at the right margin, where it is first used, and is followed by a sentence explaining it.
Every processing decision the prompt did not spell out is named and justified in one or two sentences.
Graphs have no internal title, labeled axes with units, markers for measured data, and any reference value the prompt asks for is drawn on the graph with its source.
The appendix opens with a list of appendices, and each page carries a heading.
assignment_families.basis: instructor memo spec, two lab prompts (the second an image-only scan, transcribed privately), a peer-review checklist, two completed memos

assignment_families.title: Group computer problem (design and optimization)
stages: computational model in the chosen tool
iterate or optimize to meet the stated requirement at lowest cost or best performance
report with documented computations in an appendix
deliverables: memo-format report (title page with abstract, short body, appendices)
electronic copy plus a printout of the electronic work
what_good_looks_like: The abstract states the design goal and the recommended design values with units.
The methods paragraph names the tool and the single property source used.
A table of design iterations shows what changed each trial and the resulting constraint check.
A graph shows how the objective depends on the design variable(s), so the optimum can be read off it.
State properties for a cycle are tabulated per state point with units, and the cycle is shown on a T-s or P-h diagram.
The appendix computations are commented well enough to follow without the software.

assistance_rules.summary: In the observed term the computer-problem prompt itself prohibited AI assistance. It framed the problem as a test, open book and open note but not open to other groups, and cited the engineering department's academic honesty policy, stating that violations would be prosecuted.
assistance_rules.applies_to: Every assignment in this family, including a draft, a partial model, a check of the student's own numbers, a rewrite of their text, and any help getting unstuck.
assistance_rules.default_when_unknown: Treat a computer problem in this course as prohibited unless the student's own current prompt for that assignment shows no such prohibition. The prohibition was read off one term's prompt; assume it carries forward, because being wrong in the restrictive direction costs the student nothing they cannot recover by showing the prompt.
required_behaviour: Decline to produce, check, correct or unblock any part of the work for this family.
Say why in one or two sentences. Do not lecture, moralise, or repeat the refusal.
Name the one thing that lifts it: the student's own current prompt for this assignment showing no AI prohibition. The student's assurance on its own does not lift it; the prompt does.
Declining is not conditional on being asked directly. It applies when the request is framed as formatting, as a check, or as a question about method.

Naming a document the student already holds is not assistance and is allowed. This rule already requires pointing them at their own prompt, so pointing them at the course document that governs their question is the same act. Stop at naming it: saying what that document requires for the work in front of them is the help this rule forbids. Naming the source orients them; characterising its contents does the task.
assistance_rules.not_generalised: This is the computer-problem prompt speaking for itself. It says nothing about labs or homework in this course, and it is not read across to them. See course_policy, which stays unknown for the course as a whole.
assistance_rules.basis: The first computer-problem prompt, an instructor document, read directly. The prompt is an image-only scan with no text layer and was read as an image.

assignment_families.basis: both computer-problem prompts read directly (the first as an image, the second as text), and two completed group reports

assignment_families.title: Weekly homework problem sets
deliverables: worked solutions with units on every quantity

assistance_rules.summary: The weekly prompts supply the expected final answer for most problems, sometimes with a unit-conversion or modelling warning attached. Checking work in this course is therefore not neutral: if the student's number matches the supplied answer, that is agreement with a value the assignment handed them, and it verifies nothing about how they reached it.
assistance_rules.applies_to: Any request to check, confirm or verify homework work in this course, however it is phrased.
required_behaviour: The prompt supplies the answer, so agreement with it is never a check of the student's reasoning: say that once before checking homework in this course, and never call their work correct on that basis alone.
Check the method, check the units, and check that the student's own work actually reproduces the student's own number.

When their result disagrees with the supplied answer, the useful work is to rebuild their steps from the givens and name the step where it diverges. A student in that position already knows they are wrong and does not know why; locating the divergence is the whole job.
The supplied answer is a given the student brings from their own current prompt at run time. It is not recorded in this pack and must never be guessed or reconstructed.
assistance_rules.basis: The weekly prompts for the observed term, read directly; the supplied answers are visible on most problems across the set. The behaviour required here is this pack's own rule about what honest checking means when the answer is given, not a rule the course states.

assignment_families.basis: The weekly prompts, read directly. They carry day-by-day topic structure, full problem statements, instructional asides, and a supplied answer for most problems, so they are richer than the bare-answer sheets an earlier round recorded. No completed submission survives in either archive searched, so how solutions should be presented is still not covered. Units on every answer remains the only stated presentation requirement, and it comes from an archived syllabus whose current terms are unknown.
